title: Skin and Dress Small Stock Carcasses

lessons.title: Legging, heading and opening the skin
lessons.html:
Getting ready

  • Put on clean PPE: apron, hairnet, boots, cut-resistant glove.
  • Have two sharp knives: one in use, one in the sterilizer.
  • Check that your sterilizer is hot and your hand-wash basin works.

Step 1: Front legs

  1. Open the skin on the back of the front leg from the knee towards the brisket, with the knife blade pointing outwards (cutting from the inside of the skin).
  2. Free the skin around the leg by fisting or with careful knife strokes.
  3. Remove the front foot at the knee joint.
  4. Sterilise your knife.

Step 2: Hind legs

  1. Open the skin on the inside of each hind leg from the hock towards the crotch, blade outwards.
  2. Free the skin around the hock and upper leg.
  3. Remove the hind feet at the hock joint, and transfer the leg to a hook or spreader as your plant does it.

Step 3: Neck and brisket

  1. Open the skin down the middle of the neck and brisket.
  2. Free the oesophagus (weasand) and tie it or clip it.
  3. Remove or skin the head as your plant procedure says, keeping it matched to the carcass.

Rules at every step

  • The woolly side of the skin must not touch the meat. Fold it outwards and away.
  • Sterilise the knife after each cut through the skin.
  • Wash your hands after handling wool.
  • Put feet into the foot chute, not on the floor.

lessons.title: Removing the skin
lessons.html:
Fisting the skin loose

Once the legs, neck and brisket are opened, the skin is freed from the sides, shoulders and belly by fisting: you push your closed fist between the skin and the carcass. This separates the skin without knife cuts in the meat or the skin.

  • Keep your fist close to the skin, not pushing into the meat.
  • Keep the fat cover on the carcass, not on the skin.
  • Use your knife only where the skin is stuck, holding the blade towards the skin.

Pulling the skin

Follow the method your abattoir uses:

  • Inverted method: with the carcass hanging by the front legs, the skin is pulled downwards from the shoulders over the back, hindquarters and tail, by hand or with a mechanical skin puller.
  • Traditional method: with the carcass hanging by the hind legs, the skin is pulled downwards from the hindquarters over the back and shoulders towards the neck.

Pull steadily, not in jerks. Jerking tears the fat and can flick wool onto the meat.

Freeing the tail and rectum

  1. Free the skin around the tail.
  2. Cut around the anus and free the rectum. Tie it or bag it so dung cannot escape.
  3. Sterilise the knife.

After the skin is off

  • Put the skin into the skin chute or bin straight away.
  • Look over the whole carcass for wool, hair and dirt. Trim off with a sterile knife.
  • Report any contamination you cannot remove.

Safety with skin pullers

Only trained workers operate a skin puller. Keep hands clear of chains and rollers. Know where the emergency stop is.

lessons.title: Evisceration and presenting for inspection
lessons.html:
Opening the belly

  1. Make a small cut through the belly wall near the crotch.
  2. Put two fingers inside, lift the wall away from the guts, and cut down the middle line between your fingers with the blade pointing outwards.
  3. Do not cut into the rumen or intestines.

Removing the rough offal

  1. Pull the rectum through into the belly.
  2. Lift out the stomachs and intestines together. Cut the attachments carefully.
  3. Place them on the offal tray or table matched to the carcass.

Removing the red offal

  1. Cut through the diaphragm.
  2. Open the chest if your plant does so.
  3. Remove the pluck (windpipe, heart, lungs, liver) in one piece and hang it on the matching numbered hook.

Presenting for inspection

  • Carcass, head and organs must reach the meat inspector together and matched.
  • Do not remove kidneys, lymph nodes or any abnormal part before inspection unless the procedure says so.
  • Tell the inspector about anything unusual you saw: abscesses, cysts, bruises, a bad smell.

Checking quality

Good carcassFaults to avoid
No wool, hair or dirtWool spots, dung smears
Even fat cover, no tearsTorn fat, knife scores
No gut contaminationCut rumen or intestines

Key points

  • Open the skin with the blade pointing outwards and sterilise after each cut.
  • Use fisting to free the skin and pull it steadily.
  • Keep the woolly side of the skin away from the meat.
  • Tie the weasand and bung the rectum before evisceration.
  • Open the belly with fingers protecting the guts.
  • Present carcass, head and organs together for inspection.

quiz.question: Why should the skin be opened with the knife blade pointing outwards?

options.text: To cut from the inside of the skin and avoid dragging wool and germs into the meat
To make bigger holes in the skin
So the skin is easier to sell

quiz.question: Why should the skin be pulled steadily and not in jerks?

options.text: Jerking tears the fat and can flick wool onto the meat
So the skin stays on longer

quiz.question: Where should feet go after removal?
When opening the belly, what protects the guts from the knife?

options.text: Two fingers lifting the belly wall away from the guts

quiz.question: What do you do if you see an abscess during evisceration?

options.text: Cut it out before the inspector sees it

quiz.question: Fisting frees the skin with fewer knife cuts in the meat and skin.
Lymph nodes should be removed before the carcass reaches the meat inspector.
